title: When the Brain Rewrites Reality
description: Impostor spouses, a woman sure she had no organs, and the shrinking world of Alice

concepts.title: Capgras: An Impostor With a Familiar Face
concepts.contentHtml:
Imagine looking at your husband and feeling certain that he is a stranger who merely looks exactly like him. In 1923 the French psychiatrists Capgras and Reboul-Lachaux described a patient who believed that the people around her, even her husband and daughter, had been replaced by doubles. Over a few months she complained that she had been shown one thousand doubles of her daughter.1

The Capgras delusion is puzzling because recognition still works: the patient agrees that the person looks exactly like their spouse, but insists it is someone else. The leading explanation starts with a small bodily signal. Seeing a face sets off an automatic response that shows up as a change in the skin's electrical conductance, and the response to a familiar face is considerably stronger than to a stranger's.2

In 1990 Ellis and Young proposed that in Capgras the face is recognized but this response, which marks a face as personally significant, fails. In 1997 they tested five people with the delusion: their skin conductance did not distinguish familiar faces from unfamiliar ones, although their responses to tones were normal.3 Hirstein and Ramachandran studied a man known as DS who called his parents impostors when he was looking at them, but not when he was speaking to them on the telephone. They suggested that the connections from his brain's face-processing areas to its emotional (limbic) system had been damaged.4

A missing feeling cannot be the whole story, though. People with damage to the ventromedial frontal cortex show the same flat response to familiar faces, yet they still recognize their spouses as their spouses. So researchers such as Max Coltheart argue for a second fault, in the system that should reject an impossible belief once family members keep supplying evidence against it.5

concepts.title: Cotard: The Delusion of Negation
concepts.contentHtml:
On 28 June 1880 the French physician Jules Cotard described a 43-year-old patient to the Société Médico-Psychologique. She believed that she had no brain, nerves, chest or entrails and was just skin and bone. She also said that she did not need food, and that she was eternal and would live forever.1

Cotard called this délire des négations, the delusion of negation, and he meant a form of depressive illness. Later writers narrowed his name to a single belief: that one is dead.2 When Berrios and Luque analyzed 100 published cases in 1995, depression was reported in 89%; the most common nihilistic beliefs concerned the body (86%) and existence (69%). Oddly, more than half (55%) also had delusions of immortality, like the woman Cotard described.3

It is not a single disease. A 2018 review of 12 patients at the Mayo Clinic found Cotard delusions alongside a wide range of neurological, psychiatric and medical disorders. On brain imaging, seven had lesions on the right side or on both sides of the brain, and the authors suggested that lesions in the non-dominant hemisphere may play a role. Treatments used included ECT, medication and psychotherapy, and the authors stress that effective treatments are available.4

Some researchers link Cotard to Capgras. Both may begin with the same kind of unusual experience; what differs is the explanation. Blame something outside yourself and the people around you become impostors. Blame yourself, often in the setting of depression, and you may conclude that you are dead. A 2021 report described a 23-year-old man with schizophrenia who developed Cotard syndrome and later Capgras; his symptoms improved with the drug clozapine.5

concepts.title: Alice in Wonderland Syndrome
concepts.contentHtml:
A hand resting on the table begins to feel enormous. The room seems to stretch away, or the person opposite shrinks to the size of a doll. In 1955 the British psychiatrist John Todd gave such experiences a memorable name, the syndrome of Alice in Wonderland. He chose it because the symptoms of his six patients resembled John Tenniel's illustrations of Alice in Lewis Carroll's 1865 book, and most of the patients had migraine, now or in the past. The name helped bring out symptoms that patients were often afraid to mention for fear of being thought insane.1

These are distortions rather than hallucinations. What the person perceives is really there, but its size, distance or shape comes out wrong, and the passage of time can seem to speed up or slow down.2

The causes are varied. A Spanish study of 20 children found an infection in nine (five of them Epstein-Barr virus), migraine in eight, toxins in two and epilepsy in one. Most episodes lasted under three minutes, and 80% of the children had no recurrence: the syndrome is usually benign.3

And Carroll himself? He did have migraines. In 1885 he wrote in his diary of "that odd optical affection of seeing moving fortifications followed by a headache".4 In 1952 Caro Lippman suggested that Alice's growing and shrinking might have been inspired by Carroll's own experiences. Historians consider this unproven, because the diaries do not show that he had any such episodes before he wrote the book.5

title: Phantoms of the Body
description: Limbs that linger after amputation, silent visions in failing sight, a buzz that never came

concepts.title: The Limb That Stays Behind
concepts.contentHtml:
After an arm or leg is amputated, the brain often carries on as if it were still there. According to one review, a third of patients feel sensations from the missing limb within 24 hours of surgery, and 90% within six months.1 For many the phantom also hurts. A 2020 meta-analysis covering 12,765 people estimated that 64% report phantom limb pain, about six in every ten.2

In 1992 V. S. Ramachandran and colleagues touched two people who had lost an arm and asked where they felt it. Touches on the face were felt at precise points on the phantom hand, and a drop of warm water trickling down the face was felt as warm water trickling down the phantom hand. Their explanation lies in the brain's touch map, where the hand area sits next to the face area. Deprived of its own input, the hand area seems to be invaded by its neighbors.3

In 1996 Ramachandran described an inexpensive "virtual reality box": a mirror stands upright on a table so that the reflection of the patient's intact hand appears where the phantom is felt. Of ten patients, six felt the phantom move when they moved their real hand. Five had painful clenching spasms in the phantom hand, and in four of them the mirror let them open it and relieved the spasm.4

Mirror therapy is now used in clinics. It has reduced phantom pain in many amputees, though not all, and the reasons it works are still not well understood. Seeing seems to be the key: in one trial, pain did not improve when the mirror was covered with a sheet.5

concepts.title: Charles Bonnet's Silent Visions
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1760 the Swiss naturalist Charles Bonnet wrote down what his grandfather was seeing. The old man had cataracts in both eyes and very little sight, yet he saw men, women, birds, carriages and buildings that were not there. Bonnet stressed that his grandfather was otherwise "full of health, of ingenuousness, judgement and memory".1

Today Charles Bonnet syndrome is the name for hallucinations in people who have lost a lot of their sight. The images can be patterns, or people, animals and places, moving or still, in color or black and white. They are silent: people see them but do not hear, smell or feel them, and most know they are not real. It is not caused by a mental health problem or dementia.2

It is not rare. In a large US study of older adults with age-related eye disease, followed for ten years, 12% of those who answered reported symptoms, and most of them had macular degeneration or had had cataract surgery. Yet doctors often fail to recognize it, and it is often misdiagnosed as psychosis or early dementia.3

That fear weighs on families. Judith Potts's mother, Esme, saw faceless people sitting on her sofa, and the word dementia hung in the air until a specialist confirmed the syndrome. Potts went on to found a campaign, Esme's Umbrella, to spread awareness.4

Why does the brain do this? A 1998 brain-scanning study found that hallucinations of color, faces, textures and objects matched activity in the parts of the visual cortex that specialize in those very things. Patients who hallucinated also had raised activity there that persisted between hallucinations. It is as if visual areas deprived of input from the eyes start producing images of their own.5

concepts.title: The Phone That Never Buzzed
concepts.contentHtml:
You feel your phone buzz against your leg, reach for it, and find nothing. One of the first studies of this surveyed hospital staff. In a 2010 survey at an academic medical center, 115 of the 169 staff who answered (68%) said they had felt phantom vibrations from a pager or phone. Most had started after carrying the device for between a month and a year, and 13% felt them every day.1

A stressful job seems to turn the sensation up. A study in Taiwan followed 74 medical interns through their first year on the wards. Before the internship, 78.1% had felt phantom vibrations; three months in, 95.9% had. Two weeks after the internship ended, the figure fell to 50%. Phantom ringing, hearing a ring that never came, rose even more steeply, from 27.4% to 84.9%. Oddly, the false alerts did not track the interns' anxiety or depression scores.2

Is it a hallucination? Technically yes, a perception without a stimulus, but one that most healthy people have had, and the study's authors argue that normal brain mechanisms are at work. When you are expecting an important buzz, that expectation can amplify the brain's top-down processing, its habit of interpreting signals in the light of what it predicts.3 A survey of 93 medical interns in India found that 60% had felt phantom vibrations, more often among heavy phone users and those who kept their phones on vibrate. Its authors suggest that repeated vibrations and stress heighten sensitivity, so that ordinary sensations get misread as an alert.4

The good news is that the habit can often be broken. In the 2010 survey, 39% of those affected managed to stop the phantom vibrations, by turning off vibrate mode, carrying the device somewhere else, or switching to a different device.5

title: Delusions That Spread
description: Folie à deux, the Mad Gasser of Mattoon, and Seattle's epidemic of pitted windshields

concepts.title: Folie à Deux: A Delusion for Two
concepts.contentHtml:
Most delusions are lonely. A person becomes certain of something false, and the people around them do not share it. But in 1877 two psychiatrists, Lasègue and Falret, described delusions that came in pairs, and named the condition folie à deux, "madness for two". In the classic picture a primary person with a psychotic illness, usually the dominant partner, passes a specific delusion to a secondary; the two have lived closely together in social isolation; and the secondary's borrowed beliefs fade quickly once the pair are physically separated.1

Modern cases keep the outline but blur the details. A review of 42 cases published from 1993 to 2005 found that 97.6% of pairs belonged to the same nuclear family. Married couples were the largest group, then sisters, half of them twins, and social isolation turned up in about two thirds of cases. Separation, the standard remedy, often was not enough: many secondaries had psychiatric vulnerabilities of their own, so living with the primary may trigger an illness rather than simply transplant one.2

How does a false belief jump from one mind to another? In 2013 researchers tried to build folie à deux in the lab. A confederate, playing the primary, displayed two delusional beliefs to hypnotized volunteers, and many highly hypnotizable people adopted the beliefs and made up evidence to support them. Credibility mattered: volunteers who met a confederate presented as credible stretched the delusions beyond what they had been shown.3 That fits the old clinical picture, in which the partner who is trusted most, in a world with few other voices, ends up defining what is real.

concepts.title: The Mad Gasser of Mattoon
concepts.contentHtml:
For about two weeks in September 1944, the city of Mattoon, Illinois, hunted a man nobody could find. He was known as the "Mad Anesthetist" and the "Mad Gasser". Police added night patrols, citizens kept watch, and state and federal authorities joined the search, but no one ever caught him.1

It began late on September 1, when Aline Kearney smelled something sweet in her bedroom, like garden flowers, and then found her legs paralyzed for half an hour. Her husband, home from his taxi shift, thought he saw a tall man at the window. The local Journal-Gazette put her story on the front page, and the reports multiplied: a psychology student, Donald Johnson, later counted nearly 30 police reports of people sickened by fumes. Chicago papers sent reporters, and Time and Newsweek carried the story. The only physical clue, a cloth found at one home, yielded nothing. On September 11 the paper turned skeptical ("Many Prowler Reports; Few Real"), a city commissioner declared the whole thing mass hysteria, and within days complaints had dropped sharply. A 2003 book later blamed a real local man, but no gas or gasser was ever found. Johnson's 1945 study, now cited in many textbooks, named the front-page story as the immediate cause.2

Sociologists who reexamined the case call this kind of event a collective anxiety attack. Once a threat rumor spreads far enough to become the shared definition of the situation, the belief intensifies fear and distorts perception, and the expectation of feeling sick produces real symptoms.3 The victims need not have been lying. In this view the fear itself made them ill, and the gasser existed only in the story everyone was telling.

concepts.title: Seattle's Pitted Windshields
concepts.contentHtml:
In late March 1954, drivers in Bellingham, Washington, began noticing tiny pits and dings in their windshields. Police blamed vandals with BBs or buckshot. Then the damage seemed to march south. On April 13 it struck Anacortes, where officers set up roadblocks, and the Whidbey Island Naval Air Station, where nearly 75 marines searched for five hours and found nothing. By the end of the day more than 2,000 cars had been reported damaged.1

On April 14 Seattle's newspapers carried the story on the front page, and that evening the city's own reports began. By April 15 close to 3,000 windshields had been reported pitted. Theories ranged from H-bomb fallout and cosmic rays to a powerful new Navy radio transmitter and sand-flea eggs hatching in the glass. Mayor Allan Pomeroy wired the governor and President Eisenhower for help.2

The governor asked University of Washington scientists to investigate. They surveyed cars on campus, called the damage "overly emphasized" and blamed normal driving, in which small objects strike windshields. Pits were mostly on front glass and on older cars; brand-new cars on dealers' lots had none. The pits had been there all along. What changed was that, for the first time, people looked at their windshields instead of through them. By April 17 the Washington reports had stopped.3 By April 19, pitted windshields had been reported in at least nine states and Canada, and a sociologist later pointed out that thousands of pitted cars among millions in Washington state was less than 1 percent.4

title: The Answer Was in the Hand
description: Clever Hans the counting horse, dowsing and the ideomotor effect, and facilitated communication

concepts.title: Clever Hans and the Questioner's Nod
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1904 Berlin was arguing about a horse. Clever Hans, trained by a former mathematics teacher named von Osten, answered questions by tapping a hoof: sums, fractions, dates, even words spelled out with a number code. That September a panel of 13, including a circus manager, the director of the Berlin Zoo and the psychologist Carl Stumpf, watched closely and signed a report saying they could find no tricks or intentional signals, and that the case deserved serious investigation.1

The psychologist Oskar Pfungst took it on. Fitted with large blinders, Hans failed whenever he could not see his questioner. When the questioner knew the answer, Hans was right 98% of the time; when nobody present knew it, 8%. The cue was tiny. After asking, the questioner leaned slightly forward, and once Hans reached the right number, the questioner, without meaning to, made a slight upward jerk of the head. Hans stopped.2 Pfungst then played the horse himself: of 25 people he tested, all but two made the same involuntary jerk, a movement seldom as large as a millimeter.3

The Clever Hans effect is why careful experiments are run blind. In a 2011 study, 18 detection dog teams searched areas that held no drug or explosive scent at all, after handlers were falsely told some spots were marked. The teams made 225 alerts, and handlers' beliefs shaped where they happened.4 Machines do it too: in 2019 researchers found an image classifier that spotted horses partly by a source tag printed in the corner of many horse photos.5

concepts.title: Dowsing Rods and the Ideomotor Effect
concepts.contentHtml:
Give a believer a forked stick or two bent wires, walk them over a buried pipe, and the rod dips. It feels as if it moved by itself. In March 1852 the physiologist William Carpenter told the Royal Institution that ideas could drive the muscles without any act of will. He called this the ideo-motor principle and used it to explain the divining rod and the swing of a pendulum held from the finger: the performer's expectation, not some mysterious force, moves the hand.1

The next year Michael Faraday tested table-turning, in which sitters with their hands on a table felt it move under them. A light lever between hands and table showed whether the table moved the hands or the hands moved the table. Once sitters could see it, the table stopped: aware of what their hands were doing, they could no longer fool themselves.2

The biggest dowsing test came in Germany. In 1986 the government granted 400,000 marks to Munich physicists who thought dowsing was probably real. About 500 candidates were whittled down to 43, who made 843 double-blind attempts to locate a water pipe on the floor below them in a barn. A reanalysis by J. T. Enright found the results looked like chance, the few good runs were never repeated, and most of the best dowsers would have done better by always guessing the middle of the line.3 Hans-Dieter Betz, the study's chief spokesman, maintained that the data showed a statistically significant, if very small, effect.4

The ideomotor effect is real; the force is you. In a 2012 Ouija board study, people who believed they were only guessing at yes/no questions were right 65% of the time through the board, against 50% when they answered directly.5

concepts.title: Facilitated Communication: Whose Words?
concepts.contentHtml:
In the early 1970s an Australian teacher, Rosemary Crossley, developed a way to help people who could not speak, including some with autism or cerebral palsy, to communicate. In facilitated communication (FC), a facilitator supports the person's hand while they point to letters on a board or keyboard. Douglas Biklen of Syracuse University brought it to the United States in 1989, and after his 1990 report that 21 people previously unable to communicate were typing with FC, it spread quickly through schools and universities.1

The test was simple: whose words were they? In a 1993 study at an autism program, Wheeler and colleagues showed pictures to the 12 most fluent FC users and to their 9 facilitators, sometimes the same picture and sometimes different ones. Typing alone, the participants could not name the pictures. When the two had seen different pictures, the only "correct" labels were for pictures shown to the facilitator. The facilitators were unknowingly determining what was typed. Nobody needed to be cheating, any more than a dowser does.2

A 2014 systematic review of the controlled studies found unequivocal evidence that FC messages are authored by the facilitators rather than the people with disabilities.3 As early as 1993, child psychiatrists warned that information obtained through FC should not be used to confirm or deny allegations of abuse.4 The American Speech-Language-Hearing Association lists false allegations of sexual abuse among FC's harms and calls it a discredited technique that should not be used, because its messages do not carry the person's own voice. Its position does not cover independent typing, and it backs evidence-based forms of augmentative and alternative communication.5 The problem was never that the people being facilitated had nothing to say. It was that FC put someone else's words in their place.
